analysis.one_liner: Requires foods containing or produced with genetically engineered material to say so on the label.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in either committee; it died there when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it misbranding to sell food containing, or made with, genetically engineered material unless the package carried a prominent "GENETICALLY ENGINEERED" notice [S2]. It would cover meat, dairy and poultry from animals fed genetically engineered feed, require the government to periodically test foods along the supply chain to verify labels, set civil penalties up to $100,000 per violation, and let private citizens sue to enforce the rule [S3]. Restaurant meals and medical foods would be exempt, and accidental trace contamination up to one percent would be allowed [S2]. The bill was referred to the Agriculture and Energy and Commerce Committees on the day it was introduced and never moved again [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Shoppers who want to know whether their food contains genetically engineered ingredients. The bill's stated purpose is that consumers have a right to know for reasons including potential allergen transfer, environmental concerns, and religious or ethical dietary restrictions [S3]. Producers who avoid genetic engineering, including certified organic growers, would get a government-recognized way to market that and would be exempt from the testing requirements [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Any food containing genetically engineered material, or produced with it, must carry a conspicuous "GENETICALLY ENGINEERED" notice sized like standard nutrition information, or it is misbranded under federal food law [S2].
The definition reaches food from animals that were fed genetically engineered material, so meat, dairy and eggs from those animals would also be labeled [S3].

The Secretary of Health and Human Services would be required to periodically test foods moving through the chain of distribution to check that labels are accurate, using the best available testing technology [S3].

The bill includes civil penalties up to $100,000 per violation and allows any person to bring a citizen suit to enforce the labeling rules or to sue the Secretary for failing to carry out a non-discretionary duty [S3].

The bill also regulates the opposite side: companies could not put a "non-GE" claim on a package unless it met regulations, and the regulations could not require a disclaimer saying non-GE has no bearing on safety [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Food manufacturers, retailers and biotech seed companies would bear the costs of changing labels, tracking ingredients, and testing; some of those costs would likely reach shoppers through prices. Companies would face penalties for violations, though processors who rely on good-faith written guarantees from suppliers, and farmers hit by unintended cross-contamination, would be shielded [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Food makers and biotech seed firms

drawbacks.text: The bill's definition counts food from animals that merely ate genetically engineered feed, so nearly all conventional meat, dairy and eggs in the United States would need the label even though the meat itself is not genetically engineered — a scope a supporter would have to defend as proportionate [S3].
Labeling, segregating and testing costs would fall on food companies and be passed at least partly to consumers through higher prices [S2].

Mainstream scientific agencies have treated approved genetically engineered foods as safe, so critics argue the label implies a danger the evidence does not establish; the bill's own findings rely partly on consumer desire to know rather than proven harm [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For shoppers the benefit is straightforward: a standardized, government-verified label on nearly all packaged foods, with enforcement teeth, at a time when the European Union, Japan and China already had or were building mandatory GE labeling [S3]. The cost is real but modest by food-industry standards — label redesign, supply-chain tracking and periodic testing — though the breadth of the definition (covering animals fed GE grain) means far more products would carry the label than a narrow reading would suggest. The main honest objection is that the label conveys production method, not proven safety differences, which some shoppers value and others will read as a warning.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Agriculture and Energy and Commerce Committees the day it was introduced, bounced to three subcommittees, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Dennis Kucinich introduced the Genetically Engineered Food Right to Know Act on July 29, 2008, with nine original cosponsors [S3].

It was referred the same day to the Agriculture Committee and to the Energy and Commerce Committee, and then to subcommittees — Health, and Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry, and Specialty Crops — with no further action recorded [S5].
It finished with 11 cosponsors (10 Democrats, 1 Republican) and died in committee when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food manufacturers, grocery retailers and biotech seed companies were better off, because no mandatory labeling or testing requirement took effect and no compliance costs were imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Food and biotech companies avoided labeling rules

sides.party_line_note: Eleven of the bill's twelve supporters were Democrats, with Christopher Shays of Connecticut the lone Republican; no vote was ever taken, so no opposition record exists.

industries.note: Mandatory labeling would mark products of their technology on most packaged food and require supply-chain testing, and the bill's findings fault federal agencies for allowing GE foods to market unlabeled. Avoiding such a rule preserves the status quo in which the industry's products carry no special label.

They would have to redesign labels, track genetically engineered inputs through the supply chain, and face up to $100,000 per violation; costs would flow partly to shoppers. Because the rule covers animals fed GE feed, conventional meat, dairy and egg processors would be affected too.

Organic-certified foods are exempt from the testing requirements, and the bill creates a regulated standard for "non-GE" claims, giving organic and non-GE producers a government-backed way to market that distinction.

The bill shields agricultural producers from penalties when their non-GE crops are unintentionally contaminated through no negligence of their own, easing one fear of GE-fields near conventional ones; but farmers selling GE-fed livestock products would face labeling-driven demand questions.
